guides.title: About this website
guides.subtitle: How to use these Easy Read guides

lines: A pharmacist in Adelaide made this guide.
When you see the word **we**, it means the pharmacist who runs this website.
We wrote this information in an easy to read way.
We use pictures to explain some ideas.
We wrote some important words in **bold**.
This means the letters are thicker and darker.
We explain what these words mean in the word list at the end.
This is an Easy Read summary of our website.
It only has the most important ideas.
The full website is at **www.gamsa.au**
You can ask for help to read this guide.
A friend, family member, support person or your pharmacist may be able to help you.
Some trans and gender diverse people take **hormone medicines**.
These medicines change your body over time.
Doctors call this **gender-affirming hormone therapy**.
People often have questions about these medicines, like:
- how much they cost
- what to do when a chemist has none left
- how to use them safely.
The answers are usually written for doctors and pharmacists.
They can be hard to find and hard to read.
We made this guide to help.
This guide does not tell you what medicine to take.
Your doctor or nurse decides that with you.
There is one Easy Read guide for each thing you might need to do.
You can read them in any order.
Each one can be printed or saved as a PDF.
We check the guides when the website changes.
Each guide shows the date we last checked it.

guides.title: Getting your medicine
guides.subtitle: Prescriptions, the pharmacy and your name on the label

lines: First you see a doctor or a nurse who can prescribe.
If they agree the medicine is right for you, they write a **prescription**.
A prescription is a note that lets you get the medicine.
Then you take the prescription to a pharmacy.
A pharmacy is also called a chemist.
It helps to use the same pharmacy each time.
The staff get to know you.
They can order your medicine in before you run out.
Your medicine label might show a name you do not use.
This is because the pharmacy computer uses your Medicare name.
You can ask the pharmacy to put your **preferred name** on the label.
Your preferred name is the name you want people to use.
Some staff will not know how to do this straight away.
They may need to ring the people who make their computer program.
It is okay to ask them to find out.

sections.h: If you live far from the city

lines: Country pharmacies keep less medicine on the shelf.
Ask for your medicine a week before you run out.
An **e-script** is a prescription on your phone.
You can send it to any pharmacy in Australia.
Some pharmacies will post your medicine to you.
Your doctor can see you by phone or video.
This is called **telehealth**.
Sometimes you must travel a long way to see a specialist.
If so, you may get help with the cost.
In South Australia this help is called **PATS**.

sources: content/pharmacy.json#Getting your name right on the label
content/pharmacy.json#What to tell the pharmacist, and what to avoid

guides.title: When a medicine is hard to get
guides.subtitle: Shortages and what to do

sections.h: When a medicine is hard to get

lines: Some days a medicine runs out across the whole country.
This is called a **shortage**.
It is not your fault and it is not your pharmacy's fault.
Our website checks the official shortage list every day.
It shows which hormone medicines are hard to get right now.
The **shortage** page has one card for each medicine and strength.
The card lists each **brand** that is hard to get.
It says when each brand should be back.
The newest changes are at the top.
Sometimes a **shortage** is coming soon.
The page shows the date it is expected to start.
If your medicine is hard to get:
- talk to your pharmacist early
- do not wait until you have run out
- ask them to order some in for you.
Your pharmacist may be able to give you a different **brand**.
A different brand is the same medicine in a different box.
This is safe and normal.

sources: content/dosing.json#If your medicine is hard to get
content/pharmacy.json#If you run out and have no script

guides.title: Paying for your medicine
guides.subtitle: The PBS, concession cards and Closing the Gap

lines: The government pays for most of the cost of many medicines.
This is called the **PBS**.
You pay the rest.
This part is called a **co-payment**.
In 2026, most people pay up to **${{PBS:general_copay}}** for a PBS medicine.
If you have a concession card, you pay up to **${{PBS:conc_copay}}**.
These amounts are from the PBS website, not from GAMSA: www.pbs.gov.au.
We checked them on {{PBS:checkedAtLong}}.
We check them again every month.
If you buy a lot of medicine in one year, the cost goes down.
This is called the **Safety Net**.
Ask your pharmacy to keep a record for you.
Some medicines are not on the PBS.
These cost more.
The website has a page that explains each one.
Some brands cost a bit more than others.
The extra cost is called a **brand premium**.
If you would rather not pay it, ask your pharmacist for a brand with no premium.
Swapping brands of the same medicine is normal and safe.
If the cost is too much, tell your pharmacist.
They can often help.
You are not the first person to ask.
**Closing the Gap** is a government plan.
It aims to make health fairer for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.
Part of it makes medicines cheaper.
If you are Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander, ask your doctor to sign you up.
You only need to do this once.
After that, PBS medicines cost less at any pharmacy.
If you have a concession card, they are free.

content/costs.json#Closing the Gap: lower costs for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people

guides.title: Using patches and gel
guides.subtitle: Medicine that goes on your skin

lines: A **patch** is a small sticker with medicine inside.
It goes on clean, dry skin.
The medicine goes through your skin slowly.
Most patches are changed twice a week.
Pick the same two days every week.
Put each new patch on a different spot.
Do not put a patch on your chest or breast.
Do not put it where a belt or waistband rubs.
If a patch falls off, put it back on or use a new one.
**Gel** is medicine you rub on your skin, usually once a day.
Put it where the box says.
Let it dry before you get dressed.
Wash your hands straight after.
Keep other people and pets away from the gel.
Wait until your skin is dry and covered.
This matters most for children and pregnant people.
Ask your pharmacist to show you.
You can ask to talk somewhere private.

sources: content/administration.json#Putting on and changing a patch
content/administration.json#Applying gel, and keeping it off other people

guides.title: Having an injection
guides.subtitle: What happens, and what to tell your nurse or doctor

lines: Some hormone medicines are given as an **injection**.
Some you have every few weeks.
Some you have every few months.
Tell the person giving the injection if you feel unwell.
Also tell them if an injection has made you sick before.
Tell your doctor about all your other medicines.
Testosterone can make your blood thicker.
Some medicines for diabetes, the heart or the kidneys can do this too.
If you take one of them, you may need more blood tests.
The long-acting testosterone injection is given slowly, into the side of your hip.
A doctor or nurse gives it.
In some places, a trained pharmacist can give it.
You then wait in the clinic for at least 30 minutes.
This is normal.
It is so staff can help if you have a rare reaction.
Tell staff straight away if you:
- cough a lot
- feel short of breath
- feel dizzy
- have chest pain.
After you leave, ring 000 if any of these happen.
Ask when your next injection is due before you leave.
Write it down.
The clinic may give you a page to take home.
It says what to look out for after the injection.
Some injections and implants pause your body's own sex hormones.
Zoladex, Lucrin, Eligard and Diphereline work this way.
They can change your mood.
Some people feel very low.
A very small number of people have thoughts of suicide.
Tell your doctor if your mood changes.
If you feel low or unsafe, ring Lifeline on **13 11 14**, any time.
Some people learn to give their own injections.
Only do this after a nurse or doctor has taught you.
Practise with them first.
The long-acting testosterone injection is not one you give yourself.
Never share needles.
Put used needles in a sharps bin, not in the rubbish.
Your pharmacy can tell you where to get a sharps bin.

sources: content/administration.json#Your long-acting injection: finding the right spot

guides.title: Taking tablets and capsules
guides.subtitle: Swallowing your medicine the right way

lines: Take your tablets the way your doctor told you.
Take them at about the same time each day.
Some tablets go under your tongue instead of being swallowed.
The label will say.
If you are not sure, ask your pharmacist.
If you forget a dose, take it when you remember.
If it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed one.
Never take two doses at once to catch up.
Keep tablets in their box, somewhere cool and dry, away from children.

sources: content/administration.json#Storing your medicine safely at home

guides.title: Understanding your dose
guides.subtitle: What the numbers on your medicine mean

lines: A **dose** is how much medicine you take, and how often.
It is written on your medicine label.
The numbers are in **milligrams (mg)** or **micrograms (mcg)**.
A microgram is a thousand times smaller than a milligram.
That is why a patch says 50 mcg and a tablet says 2 mg.
They are different ways of taking the medicine.
So the amounts are different.

sections.h: Why doses are different for different people

lines: Everyone is different.
Your doctor works out your dose from your blood tests and how you feel.
Someone else's dose is not your dose.
Many people start on a low dose.
The dose often goes up slowly over months.
Do not change your dose on your own.
Taking more does not make changes happen faster, and it can be unsafe.
You will have **blood tests** from time to time.
They show your doctor if the dose is right.
A blood test is not something you pass or fail.
When you have the test matters.
For many medicines, it is just before your next dose.
Your doctor will tell you the right time for you.
The lab may mark a result as high or low.
It uses the sex on your Medicare or lab record.
On hormones, this may not fit your body.
Talk to your doctor about the result.
Do not change your dose on your own.
Our Blood tests and **monitoring** page has a part for each medicine.
It shows which tests you may have, when, and what they aim for.
Each part has a blood test guide you can print.
If you want your dose changed, talk to your doctor.
That is a normal thing to ask.
You can print a log from our website.
Write down your doses, your blood tests and how you feel.
Bring it to your appointments.

guides.title: Where to get help
guides.subtitle: People who can help

lines: Take your medicine the way your doctor told you.
Take it at about the same time each day.
Some medicines are patches or gels that go on your skin.
Some are tablets you swallow.
Some are injections.
If you are not sure how to use your medicine, ask your pharmacist.
You can ask to talk somewhere private.
If you feel unwell after taking your medicine, get help.
Ring your doctor.
In an emergency, ring **000**.
If English is not your first language, you can get a free **interpreter**.
Ring **TIS National** on **131 450**.
Ask them to call your doctor or pharmacy for you.
The full website is at **www.gamsa.au**
It has a page for each medicine.
You can ring **1800MEDICARE** on **1800 633 422** to talk to a nurse.
This is free and open all day and all night.
SA Mental Health Triage helps in a mental health crisis in South Australia.
Ring **13 14 65**, any time.
If you feel low or unsafe, ring Lifeline on **13 11 14**, any time.
QLife is for LGBTIQ+ people.
Ring **1800 184 527**, 3pm to 9pm, every day.
13YARN is for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.
Ring **13 92 76**, any time.
You can tell us if something on the website is wrong or missing.
We want to fix it.

sources: content/resources.json#Care and support in South Australia

guides.title: Helping someone with their medicine
guides.subtitle: For family, friends and carers

lines: Someone you care about takes hormone medicine.
You can help them get it and keep taking it.
You do not need to understand everything about the medicine.
The medicine is theirs.
Their doctor sets the dose.
Do not change the dose or stop the medicine.
Learn the **name** of the medicine and the **brand**.
Write it down or take a photo of the box.
Know where the **prescription** is kept.
A prescription is the note from the doctor that lets you get the medicine.
Take the prescription and the person's **Medicare card**.
Take their **concession card** if they have one.
Tell the pharmacist the name the person uses.
Ask for that name on the label.
Ask if the price is the **PBS** price.
Ask if a **60-day** prescription is possible.

sections.h: If the medicine is out of stock

lines: Sometimes a medicine is hard to get.
This is called a **shortage**.
Look at the shortage page on this website.
It says which medicines are hard to get right now.
Each card lists the brands and when each one should be back.
Ask the pharmacist when more is coming.
Ask if a different brand is OK.
If a different medicine is needed, the doctor must say so.
Some people get a long-acting injection every few months.
After the injection they wait at the clinic for at least 30 minutes.
This is normal and safe.
Help them remember when the next one is due.
Write it on a calendar.
If something seems wrong, call the doctor or the pharmacist.
In an emergency call **000**.
QLife is a phone line for LGBTIQ+ people and the people who care about them.
Call **1800 184 527**, 3pm to 9pm, every day.
Or chat online at qlife.org.au.

sources: content/allies.json#How to help with their medicines

guides.title: What the medicines are
guides.subtitle: For family, friends and carers

lines: Hormones are chemicals the body makes.
Hormone medicine gives the body the hormones a person needs.
The main ones are **oestrogen** and **testosterone**.
These are ordinary medicines.
Doctors use the same medicines for menopause.
They also use them for people whose bodies make too little hormone.
Some are **patches** stuck on the skin.
Some are **gels** rubbed on the skin.
Some are tablets.
Some are injections.
A doctor or nurse gives the long-acting injection every few months.
In some places, a trained pharmacist can give it.
Some people learn to give their own injection.
Some people also take a medicine that **blocks** a hormone they do not want.
Common ones are spironolactone and cyproterone.
These are tablets.
The person and their doctor decide together.
The doctor sets the dose.
You do not need to check or change the dose.
This website has a page for each medicine.
Look at the **Medicines A to Z** page.

sources: content/administration.json#What happens at the injection appointment
content/administration.json#Your long-acting injection: finding the right spot

lines: The most common problems are not medical.
The medicine is out of stock.
The prescription has run out.
The pharmacy charges the wrong price.
This website helps with all of these.
See the **shortage** page, the **cost** page and the **pharmacy** page.
Serious problems are rare.
Regular **blood tests** find them early.
Help the person keep their doctor visits and blood tests.
Our Blood tests and **monitoring** page lists the usual tests for each medicine.
A swollen, painful leg.
Sudden trouble breathing or chest pain.
Feeling very unwell after an injection.
These need urgent help.
For anything else that worries you, call the doctor or the pharmacist.
They would rather hear from you early.
Do not change the dose.
Do not stop the medicine.
Do not share the medicine with anyone else.
Tell the doctor or pharmacist about new medicines, smoking, or anything that has changed.

guides.title: Being an ally
guides.subtitle: Support for you and the person you care about

lines: Use the name and the words the person asks you to use.
Use them with the pharmacy and the clinic too.
Let the person lead.
They decide what to share and with whom.
Help keep the prescription and the Medicare card together.
Help remember when the next medicine or injection is due.
Offer to ring pharmacies when a medicine is hard to get.
Offer to come to the injection appointment if they want you there.
TransHub has a section for allies, families and partners.
Go to transhub.org.au and choose **Allies**.
PFLAG+ Australia is a group for parents, carers and friends.
Transcend Australia supports families of trans children.
QLife is a free phone line for LGBTIQ+ people.
It is also for the people who care about them.
Call **1800 184 527**, 3pm to 9pm, every day.
Or chat online at qlife.org.au.

guides.title: When your child tells you about their gender
guides.subtitle: For parents and carers

sections.h: When your child tells you about their gender

lines: Your child may tell you they are trans, non-binary, or not sure about their gender.
Listen to them.
Thank them for telling you.
If they ask, use the name and pronouns they want.
It is OK if you make a mistake. Say sorry and keep going.
You do not need to know all the answers.
Not every young person wants medicine.
In South Australia, the Women's and Children's Hospital has a team for young people up to 17.
Your GP can send a letter to the team. This is called a **referral**.
There is usually a wait for the first appointment.
If your child is under 16, a parent or legal guardian goes to the appointments and must agree before any medicine starts.
You can call Kids Helpline any time on 1800 55 1800.
Parents can get support from groups like Transcend and PFLAG+.
If your child is in danger, call 000.
